## Albums (383)

- 1950 · Noel Rosa e Aracy de Almeida — Aracy de Almeida (Samba): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1954 · Canções Praieiras — Dorival Caymmi (Samba): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1956 · Conceição — Cauby Peixoto (Samba): The album of Cauby's biggest hit.
- 1958 · Canção do Amor Demais — Elizeth Cardoso (Bossa Nova): Songs by Tom and Vinicius with João Gilberto's guitar on two tracks; an early bossa nova landmark.
- 1959 · Chega de Saudade — João Gilberto (Bossa Nova): The record that opens bossa nova: syncopated guitar and whispered voice.
- 1959 · Estúpido Cupido — Celly Campello (Brazilian Rock): Brazil's first big rock-linked teen hit; it paved the way for Jovem Guarda.
- 1959 · Caymmi e Seu Violão — Dorival Caymmi (Samba): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1960 · O Amor, o Sorriso e a Flor — João Gilberto (Bossa Nova): Second LP, with "Samba de Uma Nota Só" and "Corcovado".
- 1961 · João Gilberto — João Gilberto (Bossa Nova): Third LP, closing bossa nova's founding trilogy.
- 1963 · The Composer of Desafinado, Plays — Tom Jobim (Bossa Nova): Jobim's first instrumental record in the US, arranged by Claus Ogerman.
- 1963 · Samba Esquema Novo — Jorge Ben Jor (Brazilian Rock): The debut that founded samba-rock, with "Mas Que Nada" and "Vem Morena".
- 1964 · Getz/Gilberto — Stan Getz & João Gilberto (Bossa Nova): Took bossa nova to the world, with "The Girl from Ipanema" and Astrud Gilberto.
- 1964 · Nara — Nara Leão (Bossa Nova): Debut, between bossa nova and hillside samba.
- 1965 · Coisas — Moacir Santos (Jazz and Instrumental): A masterpiece of Brazilian jazz.
- 1965 · Dois na Bossa — Elis Regina & Jair Rodrigues (MPB): Live album by the duo of O Fino da Bossa; a huge seller.
- 1965 · Elis — Elis Regina (MPB): First major album by the singer who defined festival-era MPB.
- 1965 · Show Opinião — Nara Leão, João do Vale e Zé Kéti (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1965 · Jovem Guarda — Roberto Carlos (Brazilian Rock): Made Roberto Carlos the teen idol and named the movement, between iê-iê-iê and ballads.
- 1966 · Herb Alpert Presents Sergio Mendes & Brasil '66 — Sérgio Mendes (Bossa Nova): The version of "Mas Que Nada" heard around the world.
- 1966 · Os Afro-Sambas — Baden Powell e Vinicius de Moraes (Bossa Nova): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1966 · Chico Buarque de Hollanda — Chico Buarque (MPB): Debut, with "A Banda" and "Olê, Olá".
- 1967 · Francis Albert Sinatra & Antônio Carlos Jobim — Frank Sinatra & Tom Jobim (Bossa Nova): Sinatra sings Jobim, with Jobim himself on guitar.
- 1967 · Wave — Tom Jobim (Bossa Nova): Instrumental, orchestral Jobim, with the title track.
- 1967 · Vibrações — Jacob do Bandolim (Choro): With Época de Ouro; one of choro's most celebrated records.
- 1967 · Quarteto Novo — Quarteto Novo (Jazz and Instrumental): Hermeto, Airto, Heraldo do Monte and Théo de Barros: baião in jazz.
- 1967 · Em Ritmo de Aventura — Roberto Carlos (Brazilian Rock): Soundtrack to the film of the same name; the peak of Jovem Guarda and of rock in the mainstream.
- 1967 · Roberto Carlos em Ritmo de Aventura — Roberto Carlos (Brazilian Rock): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1968 · Caetano Veloso — Caetano Veloso (MPB): Tropicalist solo debut, with "Alegria, Alegria" and "Tropicália".
- 1968 · Gilberto Gil — Gilberto Gil (MPB): Gil with Os Mutantes and Rogério Duprat, with "Domingo no Parque".
- 1968 · Tropicália ou Panis et Circencis — Caetano Veloso, Gilberto Gil, Gal Costa, Tom Zé, Os Mutantes e Nara Leão (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1968 · O Inimitável — Roberto Carlos (Brazilian Rock): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1968 · Os Mutantes — Os Mutantes (Brazilian Rock): Psychedelia, MPB and studio experiments, with "Panis et Circenses" and "Bat Macumba".
- 1968 · Tropicália ou Panis et Circensis — Vários Artistas (Brazilian Rock): The Tropicália manifesto, with Caetano, Gil, Gal, Tom Zé and Os Mutantes.
- 1969 · Gal Costa — Gal Costa (MPB): Tropicalist solo debut, with "Baby" and "Divino, Maravilhoso".
- 1969 · Mutantes — Os Mutantes (Brazilian Rock): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1969 · Martinho da Vila — Martinho da Vila (Samba): Debut, with "Casa de Bamba" and "O Pequeno Burguês".
- 1970 · A Bad Donato — João Donato (Jazz and Instrumental): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1970 · Roberto Carlos — Roberto Carlos (MPB): The album of "Jesus Cristo" and "Ana".
- 1970 · A Divina Comédia ou Ando Meio Desligado — Os Mutantes (Brazilian Rock): Mature psychedelia and songs that became classics.
- 1970 · A Máquina Voadora — Ronnie Von (Brazilian Rock): A rare psychedelic record joining prog and MPB.
- 1970 · Som Imaginário — Som Imaginário (Brazilian Rock): Milton Nascimento's band; psychedelia, jazz-rock and experimentalism from Minas.
- 1970 · Foi um Rio que Passou em Minha Vida — Paulinho da Viola (Samba): The album of the song-tribute to Portela.
- 1970 · Força Bruta — Jorge Ben (Samba): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1970 · Tim Maia — Tim Maia (Soul and Black Music): The debut that founded Brazilian soul, with "Azul da Cor do Mar" and "Primavera".
- 1971 · Construção — Chico Buarque (MPB): Lyrics of near-mathematical precision about life under the dictatorship.
- 1971 · Fa-Tal: Gal a Todo Vapor — Gal Costa (MPB): A live album that became a counterculture symbol.
- 1971 · Roberto Carlos — Roberto Carlos (MPB): The album of "Detalhes" and "Como Dois e Dois".
- 1971 · Carlos, Erasmo — Erasmo Carlos (Brazilian Rock): Rock'n'roll, soul and MPB in the artist's search for new sounds.
- 1971 · Jardim Elétrico — Os Mutantes (Brazilian Rock): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1971 · Tim Maia — Tim Maia (Soul and Black Music): The album of "Não Quero Dinheiro".
- 1972 · Free — Airto Moreira (Jazz and Instrumental): Brazilian percussion in CTI-label jazz.
- 1972 · Elis — Elis Regina (MPB): With Elis's first recording of "Águas de Março".
- 1972 · Expresso 2222 — Gilberto Gil (MPB): The return from exile, with "Back in Bahia" and "Oriente".
- 1972 · Acabou Chorare — Novos Baianos (Brazilian Rock): Rock and pop blended with samba, baião and choro; often ranked among Brazil's greatest records.
- 1972 · Clube da Esquina — Milton Nascimento & Lô Borges (Brazilian Rock): A double album combining music from Minas, jazz, MPB and rock.
- 1972 · Transa — Caetano Veloso (Brazilian Rock): Recorded in London exile: reggae, prog and funk with MPB.
- 1972 · A Dança da Solidão — Paulinho da Viola (Samba): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1973 · João Gilberto — João Gilberto (Bossa Nova): The "white album": voice, guitar and minimal percussion.
- 1973 · Matita Perê — Tom Jobim (Bossa Nova): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1973 · Prelude — Eumir Deodato (Jazz and Instrumental): With "Also Sprach Zarathustra (2001)", a Grammy winner.
- 1973 · Quem É Quem — João Donato (Jazz and Instrumental): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1973 · Araçá Azul — Caetano Veloso (MPB): Caetano's most experimental album.
- 1973 · Milagre dos Peixes — Milton Nascimento (MPB): An album almost without lyrics, because of censorship.
- 1973 · Pérola Negra — Luiz Melodia (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1973 · Índia — Gal Costa (MPB): Gal at her peak, with a cover censored at the time.
- 1973 · Krig-ha, Bandolo! — Raul Seixas (Brazilian Rock): Start of the solo career and of the "maluco beleza" persona; rock, baião and blues.
- 1973 · Secos & Molhados — Secos & Molhados (Brazilian Rock): Folk-rock, MPB and psychedelia with Ney Matogrosso's androgynous performance.
- 1973 · Nelson Cavaquinho — Nelson Cavaquinho (Samba): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1973 · Nervos de Aço — Paulinho da Viola (Samba): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1973 · Tim Maia — Tim Maia (Soul and Black Music): The album of "Gostava Tanto de Você".
- 1974 · Elis & Tom — Elis Regina & Tom Jobim (Bossa Nova): The Los Angeles meeting of the greatest singer and the greatest composer, with "Águas de Março".
- 1974 · Cantar — Gal Costa (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1974 · Gita — Raul Seixas (Brazilian Rock): Experimental phase, mysticism and social critique; his best-selling record.
- 1974 · Loki? — Arnaldo Baptista (Brazilian Rock): First solo record after Os Mutantes, heavy on psychedelia.
- 1974 · A Tábua de Esmeralda — Jorge Ben (Samba): Samba-rock, guitar and alchemy; Jorge Ben's most celebrated record.
- 1974 · Cartola — Cartola (Samba): The Mangueira master's recording debut, on the Marcus Pereira label.
- 1975 · Gil & Jorge: Ogum, Xangô — Gilberto Gil e Jorge Ben (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1975 · Minas — Milton Nascimento (MPB): Milton and Som Imaginário, with "Fé Cega, Faca Amolada".
- 1975 · Qualquer Coisa / Jóia — Caetano Veloso (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1975 · Refazenda — Gilberto Gil (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1975 · Revolver — Walter Franco (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1975 · Água do Céu – Pássaro — Ney Matogrosso (MPB): Ney's solo debut after Secos & Molhados.
- 1975 · Criaturas da Noite — O Terço (Brazilian Rock): Often called the greatest classic of Brazilian prog.
- 1975 · Fruto Proibido — Rita Lee & Tutti Frutti (Brazilian Rock): Cemented Rita Lee in rock, with "Ovelha Negra".
- 1975 · Lar de Maravilhas — Casa das Máquinas (Brazilian Rock): The move into prog, with esoteric themes.
- 1975 · Novo Aeon — Raul Seixas (Brazilian Rock): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1975 · Racional — Tim Maia (Brazilian Rock): Soul, funk and psychedelic rock from the Cultura Racional phase.
- 1975 · A Voz do Samba — Alcione (Samba): Debut, with "Não Deixe o Samba Morrer".
- 1975 · Claridade — Clara Nunes (Samba): With "O Mar Serenou"; a big seller.
- 1976 · Domingo, Menino Dominguinhos — Dominguinhos (Forró): One of the accordionist's key albums of the 1970s.
- 1976 · Alucinação — Belchior (MPB): The album of "Como Nossos Pais" and "Apenas um Rapaz Latino-Americano".
- 1976 · Doces Bárbaros — Caetano Veloso, Gal Costa, Gilberto Gil e Maria Bethânia (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1976 · Estudando o Samba — Tom Zé (MPB): An experimental dismantling of samba, rediscovered abroad in the 1990s.
- 1976 · Falso Brilhante — Elis Regina (MPB): From the show of the same name, with "Como Nossos Pais".
- 1976 · Guilherme Arantes — Guilherme Arantes (MPB): Debut, with "Meu Mundo e Nada Mais".
- 1976 · Meus Caros Amigos — Chico Buarque (MPB): With "O Que Será" and "Meu Caro Amigo".
- 1976 · Bixo da Seda — Bixo da Seda (Brazilian Rock): One of the first prog records from Rio Grande do Sul.
- 1976 · Jack, o Estripador — Made in Brazil (Brazilian Rock): Heavy blues and ironic lyrics; a São Paulo underground landmark.
- 1976 · Canto das Três Raças — Clara Nunes (Samba): The title track about the roots of the Brazilian people.
- 1976 · Cartola — Cartola (Samba): Second album, with "O Mundo É um Moinho" and "As Rosas Não Falam".
- 1976 · África Brasil — Jorge Ben (Samba): Samba-funk with "Taj Mahal" and "Ponta de Lança Africano".
- 1976 · Cuban Soul: 18 Kilates — Cassiano (Soul and Black Music): Brazilian soul revered by collectors.
- 1976 · Tim Maia Racional Vol. 2 — Tim Maia (Soul and Black Music): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1977 · Amoroso — João Gilberto (Bossa Nova): Standards and bossa with arrangements by Claus Ogerman.
- 1977 · Dança das Cabeças — Egberto Gismonti & Naná Vasconcelos (Jazz and Instrumental): Guitar, piano and percussion in dialogue with the forest.
- 1977 · Slaves Mass — Hermeto Pascoal (Jazz and Instrumental): The Alagoas-born "Sorcerer" in full sonic freedom.
- 1977 · Refavela — Gilberto Gil (MPB): Gil returns from Nigeria and joins afrobeat, ijexá and reggae to samba.
- 1977 · Frenéticas — Frenéticas (Brazilian Pop): The Brazilian disco era, with "Perigosa".
- 1977 · Maria Fumaça — Banda Black Rio (Soul and Black Music): Instrumental funk from the Black Rio movement.
- 1978 · Chico Buarque — Chico Buarque (MPB): With "Cálice" and "Apesar de Você", cleared by the censors.
- 1978 · Clube da Esquina 2 — Milton Nascimento (MPB): The Minas collective's second meeting, with guests such as Chico Buarque and Elis.
- 1978 · Zé Ramalho — Zé Ramalho (MPB): Debut, with "Avôhai" and "Chão de Giz".
- 1978 · Álibi — Maria Bethânia (MPB): The first album by a Brazilian woman singer to pass a million copies.
- 1978 · De Pé no Chão — Beth Carvalho (Samba): Introduced Cacique de Ramos pagode, with "Vou Festejar".
- 1979 · Ave de Prata — Elba Ramalho (Forró): Debut of the voice of forró and northeastern MPB.
- 1979 · Light as a Feather — Azymuth (Jazz and Instrumental): Brazilian jazz-funk that became a reference for DJs worldwide.
- 1979 · Angela Ro Ro — Ângela Ro Ro (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1979 · Cinema Transcendental — Caetano Veloso (MPB): With "Lua de São Jorge" and "Oração ao Tempo".
- 1979 · Essa Mulher — Elis Regina (MPB): The album of "O Bêbado e a Equilibrista".
- 1979 · Realce — Gilberto Gil (MPB): Pop and disco in Gil's own way.
- 1980 · Circense — Egberto Gismonti (Jazz and Instrumental): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1980 · Terra dos Pássaros — Toninho Horta (Jazz and Instrumental): The Minas harmony of the Clube da Esquina guitarist.
- 1980 · Alumbramento — Djavan (MPB): With "Meu Bem Querer".
- 1980 · Beleléu, Leléu, Eu — Itamar Assumpção (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1980 · Clara Crocodilo — Arrigo Barnabé (MPB): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1980 · Samba É no Fundo de Quintal — Fundo de Quintal (Samba): Debut of the group that created the language of pagode.
- 1981 · Fantasia — Gal Costa (MPB): With "Festa do Interior", one of Gal's biggest hits.
- 1982 · Cavalo de Pau — Alceu Valença (Forró): Frevo and forró with "Tropicana".
- 1982 · Luz — Djavan (MPB): Recorded in Los Angeles, with Stevie Wonder on harmonica on "Samurai".
- 1982 · As Aventuras da Blitz — Blitz (Brazilian Rock): Pop-rock, reggae and humour that set off the BRock boom.
- 1982 · Barão Vermelho — Barão Vermelho (Brazilian Rock): Raw urban-rock debut with Cazuza and Frejat.
- 1982 · Somos Apaixonados — Chitãozinho & Xororó (Sertanejo): With "Fio de Cabelo", it passed a million copies.
- 1983 · A Turma do Balão Mágico — A Turma do Balão Mágico (Children's Music): The album of "Superfantástico".
- 1983 · Camisa de Vênus — Camisa de Vênus (Brazilian Rock): Sarcasm and blunt lyrics; a classic of protest rock.
- 1983 · Cinema Mudo — Os Paralamas do Sucesso (Brazilian Rock): The band's blueprint: ska, reggae and rock, with "Vital e Sua Moto".
- 1984 · Crucificados Pelo Sistema — Ratos de Porão (Brazilian Rock): Regarded as Latin America's first punk-hardcore album.
- 1984 · Fullgás — Marina Lima (Brazilian Rock): A great 1980s pop-rock record that opened room for women in rock.
- 1984 · O Passo do Lui — Os Paralamas do Sucesso (Brazilian Rock): Eight of its ten tracks became radio hits.
- 1984 · Titãs — Titãs (Brazilian Rock): Debut of the eight-piece line-up, punk and new wave with "Sonífera Ilha".
- 1984 · Mistura Brasileira — Agepê (Samba): With "Deixa Eu Te Amar"; it passed a million copies.
- 1985 · Magia — Luiz Caldas (Axé and Bahian Music): The album of "Fricote", axé's starting point.
- 1985 · Educação Sentimental — Kid Abelha (Brazilian Rock): Delicate pop-rock with "Fixação" and "Como Eu Quero".
- 1985 · Exagerado — Cazuza (Brazilian Rock): Solo debut and the start of his approach to MPB.
- 1985 · Legião Urbana — Legião Urbana (Brazilian Rock): Renato Russo as the voice of a generation; post-punk and new wave.
- 1985 · Mais Podres do que Nunca — Garotos Podres (Brazilian Rock): Essential Brazilian punk, with "Papai Noel Velho Batuta".
- 1985 · Nós Vamos Invadir Sua Praia — Ultraje a Rigor (Brazilian Rock): Acid humour and critical lyrics; the first gold and platinum record of Brazilian rock.
- 1985 · Revoluções por Minuto — RPM (Brazilian Rock): Synthesizers and polished production; a huge seller.
- 1985 · Televisão — Titãs (Brazilian Rock): Poppier and more accessible; a critique of the media.
- 1985 · Instrumental — Almir Sater (Sertanejo): Instrumental viola caipira; a reference for generations of players.
- 1986 · Xou da Xuxa — Xuxa (Children's Music): One of the best-selling albums in Brazilian history.
- 1986 · Cabeça Dinossauro — Titãs (Brazilian Rock): Angry and political; for many critics the greatest album of the 1980s.
- 1986 · Capital Inicial — Capital Inicial (Brazilian Rock): Punk and post-punk, with "Música Urbana" and "Veraneio Vascaína".
- 1986 · Cidade Em Torrente — Biquini Cavadão (Brazilian Rock): Established the band in Brazilian pop rock.
- 1986 · Dois — Legião Urbana (Brazilian Rock): The band's biggest hit, with "Tempo Perdido" and "Eduardo e Mônica"; over a million copies.
- 1986 · Longe Demais das Capitais — Engenheiros do Hawaii (Brazilian Rock): Debut from Rio Grande do Sul, existential lyrics; landmark of the "gaúcho invasion".
- 1986 · O Concreto Já Rachou — Plebe Rude (Brazilian Rock): A political mini-LP produced by Herbert Vianna.
- 1986 · O Futuro É Vortex — Os Replicantes (Brazilian Rock): Fast, furious punk, with "Surfista Calhorda".
- 1986 · Pela Paz em Todo Mundo — Cólera (Brazilian Rock): Political, pacifist punk; an independent-label success.
- 1986 · Rádio Pirata ao Vivo — RPM (Brazilian Rock): A live, keyboard-heavy recording; one of the industry's biggest sellers.
- 1986 · Selvagem? — Os Paralamas do Sucesso (Brazilian Rock): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1986 · Vivendo e Não Aprendendo — Ira! (Brazilian Rock): Established Edgard Scandurra as a songwriter; post-punk and pop rock.
- 1986 · Zeca Pagodinho — Zeca Pagodinho (Samba): Solo debut, which established Zeca as the voice of pagode.
- 1986 · Roberta Miranda — Roberta Miranda (Sertanejo): Debut, with "Majestade, o Sabiá".
- 1987 · Egito Madagascar — Olodum (Axé and Bahian Music): Olodum's debut, with "Faraó (Divindade do Egito)".
- 1987 · A Revolta dos Dândis — Engenheiros do Hawaii (Brazilian Rock): Defined the band's sound; a fan favourite.
- 1987 · Vida Bandida — Lobão (Brazilian Rock): Rock, pop and new wave with "Vida Bandida" and "Me Chama".
- 1988 · Xou da Xuxa 3 — Xuxa (Children's Music): With "Ilariê"; often cited as the best-selling album in the country's history.
- 1988 · Ideologia — Cazuza (Brazilian Rock): Among his most acclaimed, with "Ideologia", "Brasil" and "Faz Parte do Meu Show".
- 1988 · O Tempo Não Para (Ao Vivo) — Cazuza (Brazilian Rock): Iconic live album of the solo years, with songs that became anthems.
- 1988 · Os Cascavelletes — Os Cascavelletes (Brazilian Rock): Acid humour and eroticism in rockabilly, garage and punk.
- 1988 · Ouça o que Eu Digo: Não Ouça Ninguém — Engenheiros do Hawaii (Brazilian Rock): Gessinger's philosophical lyrics, with "Terra de Gigantes".
- 1988 · Psicoacústica — Ira! (Brazilian Rock): One of the band's most experimental albums.
- 1988 · Ed Motta & Conexão Japeri — Ed Motta (Soul and Black Music): Debut, with "Manuel".
- 1989 · Funk Brasil — DJ Marlboro (Brazilian Funk): The compilation that introduced funk carioca sung in Portuguese.
- 1989 · MM — Marisa Monte (MPB): Live debut, with "Bem Que Se Quis".
- 1989 · As Quatro Estações — Legião Urbana (Brazilian Rock): The introspective phase, with "Pais e Filhos".
- 1989 · Theatre of Fate — Viper (Brazilian Rock): The first Brazilian melodic metal to draw attention abroad.
- 1989 · Õ Blésq Blom — Titãs (Brazilian Rock): Peak of the band's golden era in production and range.
- 1990 · Holocausto Urbano — Racionais MC's (Rap and Hip-Hop): The group's debut, with "Pânico na Zona Sul".
- 1990 · O Papa é Pop — Engenheiros do Hawaii (Brazilian Rock): A poppier, more commercial sound; a 1990s hit.
- 1990 · Cowboy do Asfalto — Chitãozinho & Xororó (Sertanejo): The album of "Evidências".
- 1990 · Leandro & Leonardo Vol. 4 — Leandro & Leonardo (Sertanejo): With "Pense em Mim"; sales in the millions.
- 1991 · Mais — Marisa Monte (MPB): Produced by Arto Lindsay; the new MPB of the 1990s starts here.
- 1991 · Tudo Ao Mesmo Tempo Agora — Titãs (Brazilian Rock): Experimental and heavy; it surprised critics and fans.
- 1991 · Zezé Di Camargo & Luciano — Zezé Di Camargo & Luciano (Sertanejo): Debut, with "É o Amor".
- 1992 · O Canto da Cidade — Daniela Mercury (Axé and Bahian Music): Axé takes the country, with the title track and "Swing da Cor".
- 1992 · Acústico MTV — Legião Urbana (Brazilian Rock): The band's best-selling album and one of the country's most iconic.
- 1992 · Skank — Skank (Brazilian Rock): Rock, ska and reggae debut, with "Garganta".
- 1993 · Timbalada — Timbalada (Axé and Bahian Music): Debut of Carlinhos Brown's timbau drummers, with "Beija-Flor".
- 1993 · Gabriel o Pensador — Gabriel o Pensador (Rap and Hip-Hop): Debut, with "Tô Feliz (Matei o Presidente)" and "Lôraburra".
- 1993 · Angels Cry — Angra (Brazilian Rock): Power metal and classical music, with Andre Matos's voice.
- 1993 · Chaos A.D. — Sepultura (Brazilian Rock): A watershed: tribal and industrial music inside thrash metal.
- 1994 · Música de Rua — Daniela Mercury (Axé and Bahian Music): Daniela's follow-up to "O Canto da Cidade".
- 1994 · Verde, Anil, Amarelo, Cor-de-Rosa e Carvão — Marisa Monte (MPB): Samba, pop and song in one of Marisa's best-selling albums.
- 1994 · Sobre Todas as Forças — Cidade Negra (Brazilian Reggae): The first album with Toni Garrido, featuring "Onde Você Mora?".
- 1994 · Calango — Skank (Brazilian Rock): Over a million copies; it cemented the band's sound.
- 1994 · Cássia Eller — Cássia Eller (Brazilian Rock): Rock, pop and MPB, with "Malandragem".
- 1994 · Da Lama ao Caos — Chico Science & Nação Zumbi (Brazilian Rock): The founding work of manguebeat: rock, maracatu and social critique.
- 1994 · O Rappa — O Rappa (Brazilian Rock): A debut centred on social critique, police violence and racism.
- 1994 · Raimundos — Raimundos (Brazilian Rock): Ramones-style punk with forró; around 200,000 copies.
- 1994 · Samba Esquema Noise — Mundo Livre S/A (Brazilian Rock): Electronics, maracatu, samba and rock; another manguebeat landmark.
- 1995 · Mamonas Assassinas — Mamonas Assassinas (Brazilian Rock): The band's only album; humour and parody, a sales phenomenon.
- 1995 · Usuário — Planet Hemp (Brazilian Rock): Skate-punk and rap-rock for legalization; a gold record.
- 1996 · Alfagamabetizado — Carlinhos Brown (Axé and Bahian Music): Carlinhos Brown's solo debut, with "A Namorada".
- 1996 · Na Cabeça e na Cintura — É o Tchan (Axé and Bahian Music): Pagode baiano among the best-selling records of the 1990s.
- 1996 · Claudinho & Buchecha — Claudinho & Buchecha (Brazilian Funk): The funk melody debut, with "Nosso Sonho" and "Conquista".
- 1996 · Canções de Brincar — Palavra Cantada (Children's Music): Quality children's music that became a reference in schools.
- 1996 · Festa do Boi Bumbá — Carrapicho (Folk Traditions): The album of "Tic, Tic, Tac", certified platinum.
- 1996 · Afrociberdelia — Chico Science & Nação Zumbi (Brazilian Rock): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1996 · Jota Quest — Jota Quest (Brazilian Rock): Pop, funk and rock, with "Encontrar Alguém" and "Daqui pra Frente".
- 1996 · Roots — Sepultura (Brazilian Rock): A global metal classic with Indigenous music and Brazilian rhythms.
- 1996 · Sobre Todas as Forças — Cidade Negra (Brazilian Rock): Reggae and MPB, with "Onde Você Mora".
- 1996 · Tem Mas Acabou — Pato Fu (Brazilian Rock): First half of a two-album, retro-sounding project.
- 1997 · 2 IHU – Kewere: Rezar — Marlui Miranda (Indigenous Music): Indigenous songs recorded live at Sesc Pompeia, São Paulo.
- 1997 · Livro — Caetano Veloso (MPB): Winner of the Grammy for World Music.
- 1997 · Por Onde Andará Stephen Fry? — Zeca Baleiro (MPB): Debut, with "Salão de Beleza".
- 1997 · Sobrevivendo no Inferno — Racionais MC's (Rap and Hip-Hop): The most important Brazilian rap album, with "Diário de um Detento".
- 1997 · Natiruts — Natiruts (Brazilian Reggae): Debut, with "Liberdade pra Dentro da Cabeça".
- 1997 · A Sétima Efervescência — Júpiter Maçã (Brazilian Rock): Psychedelic and experimental; indie avant-garde.
- 1997 · Acústico MTV — Titãs (Brazilian Rock): Intimate versions with Caetano Veloso and Marina Lima.
- 1997 · Transpiração Contínua Prolongada — Charlie Brown Jr. (Brazilian Rock): Debut with around 250,000 copies and "Proibida pra Mim".
- 1997 · Só Pra Contrariar — Só Pra Contrariar (Samba): One of the best-selling records in the country's history, with "Que Se Chama Amor".
- 1998 · Diante do Trono — Diante do Trono (Gospel and Religious Music): The Minas group's debut, recorded live in Belo Horizonte.
- 1998 · Músicas para Louvar ao Senhor — Padre Marcelo Rossi (Gospel and Religious Music): Over 3 million copies; one of the country's best-selling records.
- 1998 · Carnaval na Obra — Mundo Livre S/A (Brazilian Rock): One of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums (Rolling Stone Brasil, 2007).
- 1998 · Volume Dois — Titãs (Brazilian Rock): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 1999 · Ivete Sangalo — Ivete Sangalo (Axé and Bahian Music): Solo debut after Banda Eva.
- 1999 · Banda Calypso Vol. 1 — Banda Calypso (Brega, Calypso and Sounds of Pará): An independent debut that spread across the North and Northeast.
- 1999 · São Paulo Confessions — Suba (Electronic): Electronics and MPB by the Serbian producer based in São Paulo.
- 1999 · Ana Carolina — Ana Carolina (MPB): Debut, with "Garganta".
- 1999 · Djavan ao Vivo — Djavan (MPB): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 1999 · Na Pressão — Lenine (MPB): Percussive guitar and urban lyrics from the Northeast.
- 1999 · As Quatro Estações — Sandy & Junior (Brazilian Pop): The duo's teen-pop peak, with millions of copies.
- 1999 · Lado B Lado A — O Rappa (Brazilian Rock): Experimental and heavy, with Marcelo Yuka's social lyrics.
- 1999 · Preço Curto, Prazo Longo — Charlie Brown Jr. (Brazilian Rock): Over 250,000 copies and "Zóio de Lula".
- 1999 · Só No Forevis — Raimundos (Brazilian Rock): Forró and carimbó inside punk, with "Mulher de Fases".
- 2000 · Tanto Tempo — Bebel Gilberto (Bossa Nova): Electronic bossa nova that sold worldwide.
- 2000 · Deixa Entrar — Falamansa (Forró): Debut of university forró, with "Xote da Alegria"; sold millions.
- 2000 · Memórias, Crônicas e Declarações de Amor — Marisa Monte (MPB): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2000 · Rap É Compromisso — Sabotage (Rap and Hip-Hop): The only album released in his lifetime by the "Maestro do Canão".
- 2000 · Ilegal — Tihuana (Brazilian Rock): Rock, reggae and rap, with "Que Ves?".
- 2000 · Nadando com os Tubarões — Charlie Brown Jr. (Brazilian Rock): Youth and social themes, with "Não é Sério" featuring Negra Li.
- 2001 · Bonde do Tigrão — Bonde do Tigrão (Brazilian Funk): Funk carioca on network TV in the early 2000s.
- 2001 · Kelly Key — Kelly Key (Brazilian Pop): Debut, with "Baba".
- 2001 · 100% Charlie Brown Jr. – Abalando a Sua Fábrica — Charlie Brown Jr. (Brazilian Rock): Skate punk, rap and hardcore, with "Lugar ao Sol".
- 2001 · Acústico MTV — Cássia Eller (Brazilian Rock): A posthumous album that confirmed the singer's power.
- 2001 · Ao Vivo MTV — Skank (Brazilian Rock): Unplugged versions; one of the band's biggest sellers.
- 2001 · Bloco do Eu Sozinho — Los Hermanos (Brazilian Rock): A step toward a more complex, mature sound.
- 2001 · Rebirth — Angra (Brazilian Rock): A new chapter with a new line-up, with "Nova Era".
- 2001 · Acústico ao Vivo — Bruno & Marrone (Sertanejo): The album that took the duo nationwide, with "Dormi na Praça".
- 2002 · Fernanda Porto — Fernanda Porto (Electronic): Debut, with "Sambassim", MPB and drum'n'bass.
- 2002 · Tribalistas — Tribalistas (MPB): Marisa Monte, Arnaldo Antunes and Carlinhos Brown; a hit without concerts.
- 2002 · Rouge — Rouge (Brazilian Pop): The Popstars girl group, with "Ragatanga"; millions of copies.
- 2002 · Nada Como um Dia Após o Outro Dia — Racionais MC's (Rap and Hip-Hop): A double album with "Negro Drama" and "Vida Loka".
- 2002 · Bocas Ordinárias — Charlie Brown Jr. (Brazilian Rock): More rock'n'roll, with "Papo Reto" on the radio.
- 2002 · Chegou A Hora de Recomeçar — CPM 22 (Brazilian Rock): Cemented melodic hardcore, with "Dias Atrás" and "Regina Let's Go".
- 2002 · Ritual — Shaman (Brazilian Rock): Melodic metal with Brazilian influences, by former Angra members.
- 2002 · Deixa a Vida Me Levar — Zeca Pagodinho (Samba): The title track became the national team's anthem in the 2002 World Cup win.
- 2003 · Quero Me Apaixonar — Diante do Trono (Gospel and Religious Music): Recorded live before a huge crowd; one of the country's best-selling gospel albums.
- 2003 · Maria Rita — Maria Rita (MPB): Debut, with "A Festa"; a big seller.
- 2003 · À Procura da Batida Perfeita — Marcelo D2 (Rap and Hip-Hop): Samba and rap, produced by Mario Caldato Jr.
- 2003 · Acústico MTV — Charlie Brown Jr. (Brazilian Rock): Unplugged versions that became a landmark in the catalogue.
- 2003 · Admirável Chip Novo — Pitty (Brazilian Rock): A debut that brought a powerful female voice back to rock.
- 2003 · Detonautas — Detonautas (Brazilian Rock): Alternative protest rock.
- 2003 · Ventura — Los Hermanos (Brazilian Rock): Creative peak: rock and MPB with complex arrangements.
- 2003 · Acústico MTV — Zeca Pagodinho (Samba): Pagode classics in acoustic versions; a huge seller.
- 2004 · MTV ao Vivo — Ivete Sangalo (Axé and Bahian Music): Recorded at the Fonte Nova stadium in Salvador; one of her best-selling albums.
- 2004 · Essa Boneca Tem Manual — Vanessa da Mata (MPB): With "Ai, Ai, Ai".
- 2004 · Babylon by Gus Vol. 1: O Ano do Macaco — Black Alien (Rap and Hip-Hop): A cult classic of Rio rap.
- 2004 · Zero e Um — Dead Fish (Brazilian Rock): A landmark of Brazilian hardcore, committed and powerful.
- 2005 · Ana & Jorge — Ana Carolina e Seu Jorge (MPB): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2005 · Pista Livre — Cachorro Grande (Brazilian Rock): Direct garage rock with classic-rock and blues roots.
- 2006 · Brasilianos — Hamilton de Holanda (Choro): The ten-string mandolin between choro and jazz.
- 2006 · Cansei de Ser Sexy — CSS (Electronic): Indie-electro in English released by Sub Pop.
- 2006 · Canto dos Malditos Na Terra do Nunca — Canto dos Malditos Na Terra do Nunca (Brazilian Rock): A melancholy debut from Bahia, post-punk and grunge.
- 2006 · Ciano — Fresno (Brazilian Rock): A seminal Brazilian emo record.
- 2006 · NX Zero — NX Zero (Brazilian Rock): Took the band into emo and pop-punk mainstream.
- 2007 · Multishow ao Vivo: Ivete no Maracanã — Ivete Sangalo (Axé and Bahian Music): The concert at a packed Maracanã.
- 2007 · Chromophobia — Gui Boratto (Electronic): Melodic techno released by Germany's Kompakt.
- 2007 · Desvio de Conduta — Strike (Brazilian Rock): A symbol of Brazilian pop punk, with rock, pop and reggae.
- 2007 · Samba Meu — Maria Rita (Samba): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2007 · Ao Vivo em Goiânia — Jorge & Mateus (Sertanejo): The album that launched the duo, with "Pode Chorar".
- 2008 · Agora — NX Zero (Brazilian Rock): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2008 · Ao Vivo em Uberlândia — Victor & Leo (Sertanejo): Romantic sertanejo universitário at the top.
- 2009 · Uma Nova História — Fernandinho (Gospel and Religious Music): The worship album that took over the churches, with the title track.
- 2009 · Maria Gadú — Maria Gadú (MPB): Debut, with "Shimbalaiê".
- 2009 · C_Mpl_Te — Móveis Coloniais de Acaju (Brazilian Rock): Rock, MPB and orchestral elements from the indie scene.
- 2009 · Gloria — Gloria (Brazilian Rock): Heavy sound and striking lyrics; a metalcore reference.
- 2009 · Life Is A Big Holiday For Us — Black Drawing Chalks (Brazilian Rock): Stoner, hard rock and blues rock.
- 2009 · Ao Vivo — Luan Santana (Sertanejo): The album that made Luan sertanejo's teen idol.
- 2010 · Apanhador Só — Apanhador Só (Brazilian Rock): Experimental and inventive; a highlight of the "new Brazilian rock".
- 2011 · Extraordinário Amor de Deus — Aline Barros (Gospel and Religious Music): With "Ressuscita-me".
- 2011 · O Que Você Quer Saber de Verdade — Marisa Monte (MPB): With "Ainda Bem".
- 2011 · Nó na Orelha — Criolo (Rap and Hip-Hop): Rap, samba, afrobeat and reggae with "Não Existe Amor em SP".
- 2011 · Seiva — Rancore (Brazilian Rock): A landmark of melodic, experimental hardcore.
- 2011 · Na Balada — Michel Teló (Sertanejo): The album of "Ai Se Eu Te Pego", No. 1 in over 20 countries.
- 2012 · Treme — Gaby Amarantos (Brega, Calypso and Sounds of Pará): Pará tecnobrega on record, with "Ex Mai Love".
- 2012 · Brasileiro — Nelson Freire (Classical Music): Villa-Lobos and other Brazilian composers played by the pianist, released by Decca.
- 2012 · Tudo Tanto — Tulipa Ruiz (MPB): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2012 · Fast Relief — Garage Fuzz (Brazilian Rock): Direct melodic hardcore with memorable riffs.
- 2012 · O Pensamento É Um Imã — Vivendo do Ócio (Brazilian Rock): Poetic lyrics that established the band in indie rock.
- 2013 · Raridade — Anderson Freire (Gospel and Religious Music): The album of the title track, one of the most sung worship songs of the decade.
- 2013 · Condição Humana — Guilherme Arantes (MPB): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2013 · Anitta — Anitta (Brazilian Pop): Debut, with "Show das Poderosas".
- 2013 · Batuk Freak — Karol Conká (Rap and Hip-Hop): Debut, with "Boa Noite".
- 2013 · O Glorioso Retorno de Quem Nunca Esteve Aqui — Emicida (Rap and Hip-Hop): Studio debut, with "Levanta e Anda".
- 2013 · Real / Surreal — Scalene (Brazilian Rock): Post-stoner, alternative and progressive.
- 2014 · Feitiço Caboclo — Dona Onete (Brega, Calypso and Sounds of Pará): "Chamegado" carimbó recorded after the age of 70.
- 2014 · Convoque Seu Buda — Criolo (Rap and Hip-Hop): Rap, samba and afrobeat after "Nó na Orelha".
- 2014 · Cores & Valores — Racionais MC's (Rap and Hip-Hop): The group's return after twelve years.
- 2014 · Amianto — Supercombo (Brazilian Rock): Indie, alternative and emocore with emotional lyrics.
- 2014 · Banda do Mar — Banda do Mar (Brazilian Rock): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2014 · Modehuman — Far From Alaska (Brazilian Rock): Heavy, energetic sound, stoner and alternative metal.
- 2014 · Ao Vivo em Brasília — Henrique & Juliano (Sertanejo): The album that put the duo at the top.
- 2015 · A Mulher do Fim do Mundo — Elza Soares (MPB): Elza reinvented with São Paulo's avant-garde; a Latin Grammy winner.
- 2015 · Bang — Anitta (Brazilian Pop): Funk pop and electronic, with the title track.
- 2015 · Sobre Crianças, Quadris, Pesadelos e Lições de Casa — Emicida (Rap and Hip-Hop): Recorded across Angola, Cape Verde and Brazil.
- 2015 · Fortaleza — Cidadão Instigado (Brazilian Rock): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2015 · III — Maglore (Brazilian Rock): Alternative rock, MPB and folk.
- 2015 · Manual ou Guia Livre de Dissolução dos Sonhos — Boogarins (Brazilian Rock): Organic psychedelia between rock, pop and MPB.
- 2015 · Éter — Scalene (Brazilian Rock): Intensity and atmosphere; a Latin Grammy winner.
- 2016 · Duas Cidades — BaianaSystem (Axé and Bahian Music): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2016 · A Danada Sou Eu — Ludmilla (Brazilian Funk): Funk pop with "Bom".
- 2016 · Anavitória — Anavitória (MPB): Debut, with "Trevo (Tu)".
- 2016 · Boogie Naipe — Mano Brown (Rap and Hip-Hop): The soul and funk solo album by Racionais' leader.
- 2016 · Ao Vivo — Marília Mendonça (Sertanejo): The album of "Infiel"; the start of feminejo.
- 2016 · Ao Vivo em Goiânia — Maiara & Maraisa (Sertanejo): The album of "10%" and "Medo Bobo".
- 2016 · Remonta — Liniker (Soul and Black Music): Debut of the band Liniker e os Caramelows.
- 2017 · Pirata — BaianaSystem (Axé and Bahian Music): Guitarra baiana, dub and activism from Salvador.
- 2017 · Letrux em Noite de Climão — Letrux (MPB): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2017 · Recomeçar — Tim Bernardes (MPB): Solo debut by O Terno's voice.
- 2017 · Vai Passar Mal — Pabllo Vittar (Brazilian Pop): Debut, with "K.O." and "Todo Dia".
- 2017 · Esú — Baco Exu do Blues (Rap and Hip-Hop): Debut by the Bahian rapper.
- 2017 · Galanga Livre — Rincon Sapiência (Rap and Hip-Hop): Rap and Afro-Brazilian rhythms.
- 2017 · Heresia — Djonga (Rap and Hip-Hop): Debut, the first of an album a year.
- 2017 · Continental — Bullet Bane (Brazilian Rock): Aggressive post-hardcore with social lyrics.
- 2017 · Ego Kill Talent — Ego Kill Talent (Brazilian Rock): Members swap instruments; international recognition.
- 2017 · Lá Vem a Morte — Boogarins (Brazilian Rock): Atmospheric psychedelia recalling the 60s and 70s.
- 2017 · Xenia — Xênia França (Soul and Black Music): Solo debut, between R&B and Afro-Bahian roots.
- 2018 · Casas — Rubel (MPB): Folk and MPB with rap and samples.
- 2018 · Taurina — Anelis Assumpção (MPB): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2018 · Dona de Mim — Iza (Brazilian Pop): Debut, with "Pesadão" and the title track.
- 2018 · Sinto Muito — Duda Beat (Brazilian Pop): Debut of Recife's "sofrência pop".
- 2018 · Bluesman — Baco Exu do Blues (Rap and Hip-Hop): Rap and soul about Blackness; awarded at Cannes Lions with the short film "Bluesman".
- 2018 · Gigantes — BK' (Rap and Hip-Hop): The album that established BK' in Rio rap.
- 2018 · O Embaixador — Gusttavo Lima (Sertanejo): The live album that gave the singer his nickname.
- 2019 · Hello Mundo — Ludmilla (Brazilian Funk): Ludmilla's first live album.
- 2019 · Little Electric Chicken Heart — Ana Frango Elétrico (MPB): Psychedelic pop and MPB.
- 2019 · Kisses — Anitta (Brazilian Pop): Anitta's multilingual album, with tracks in Portuguese, Spanish and English.
- 2019 · Abaixo de Zero: Hello Hell — Black Alien (Rap and Hip-Hop): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.
- 2019 · AmarElo — Emicida (Rap and Hip-Hop): Rap, samba and MPB in dialogue with Black history; a Netflix film.
- 2019 · Ladrão — Djonga (Rap and Hip-Hop): Third album, one a year since "Heresia".
- 2019 · <atrás/além> — O Terno (Brazilian Rock): One of the band's most mature works, about existence and time.
- 2019 · Violeta — Terno Rei (Brazilian Rock): Melancholy, nostalgic indie rock.
- 2019 · Todos os Cantos — Marília Mendonça (Sertanejo): Free concerts across Brazilian capitals; the peak of feminejo.
- 2020 · Máquina do Tempo — Matuê (Rap and Hip-Hop): The trap album that broke debut records on Spotify Brazil.
- 2020 · O Líder em Movimento — BK' (Rap and Hip-Hop): Rio rap with wide impact.
- 2020 · Numanice — Ludmilla (Samba): The funk star turns to romantic pagode.
- 2020 · Bom Mesmo É Estar Debaixo D'Água — Luedji Luna (Soul and Black Music): Jazz, soul and MPB; released with a film.
- 2021 · Eu Tenho a Senha — João Gomes (Forró): The debut of romantic piseiro.
- 2021 · De Primeira — Marina Sena (MPB): Pop, funk and MPB from Minas that went viral with "Por Supuesto".
- 2021 · Batidão Tropical — Pabllo Vittar (Brazilian Pop): Pabllo revisits the tecnobrega and electronic forró of the North and Northeast.
- 2021 · Doce 22 — Luísa Sonza (Brazilian Pop): Contemporary Brazilian pop in many colours.
- 2021 · Gracinha — Manu Gavassi (Brazilian Pop): A visual album with a short film.
- 2021 · Pirata — Jão (Brazilian Pop): The album that took Jão to stadiums.
- 2022 · Sim Sim Sim — Bala Desejo (MPB): Tropicália revisited by Rio's new generation; a Latin Grammy winner.
- 2022 · Lady Leste — Gloria Groove (Brazilian Pop): With "Vermelho" and "A Queda".
- 2022 · Versions of Me — Anitta (Brazilian Pop): The album of the global hit "Envolver".
- 2022 · Quantas Vezes Você Já Foi Amado? — Baco Exu do Blues (Rap and Hip-Hop): Rap about affection and mental health.
- 2022 · Ascensão — Black Pantera (Brazilian Rock): Thrash with lyrics on racism, intolerance and activism.
- 2022 · Indigo Borboleta Anil — Liniker (Soul and Black Music): Soul and MPB; the first trans artist to win a Latin Grammy.
- 2023 · Vilã — Ludmilla (Brazilian Funk): Funk, R&B and pop.
- 2023 · Vício Inerente — Marina Sena (MPB): Second album, after "De Primeira".
- 2023 · Afrodhit — Iza (Brazilian Pop): Second album, with Afro-Brazilian influences.
- 2023 · Escândalo Íntimo — Luísa Sonza (Brazilian Pop): With "Chico"; debut records on Spotify Brazil.
- 2023 · Super — Jão (Brazilian Pop): The album of Jão's stadium tour.
- 2023 · Dos Prédios — Veigh (Rap and Hip-Hop): São Paulo trap at the top of the platforms.
- 2023 · Xande Canta Caetano — Xande de Pilares (Samba): Caetano Veloso's songs in samba.
- 2023 · Decretos Reais — Marília Mendonça (Sertanejo): Recordings released after the singer's death.
- 2024 · Funk Generation — Anitta (Brazilian Funk): Anitta returns to funk carioca for a global audience.
- 2024 · 333 — Matuê (Rap and Hip-Hop): Matuê's return, four years after "Máquina do Tempo".
- 2024 · Caju — Liniker (Soul and Black Music): Nominated for seven Latin Grammys, including Album of the Year.
- 2025 · Dominguinho — João Gomes, Mestrinho e Jota.pê (Forró): Album of the year at the Prêmio Multishow.

## Awards

- [Grammy Latino](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/grammy-latino.html) (since 2000; organiser: Latin Recording Academy (US)): It has categories dedicated to Portuguese-language music: best rock or alternative album, contemporary pop, MPB, samba/pagode, sertanejo, roots, Portuguese-language song, urban performance and Christian music. It is the most prestigious international award for Brazilian artists.
- [Prêmio Multishow de Música Brasileira](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/premio-multishow-de-musica-brasileira.html) (since 1994; organiser: Multishow channel (Globo)): The country's most visible popular award, with public and expert-jury votes; televised ceremony every year.
- [Prêmio da Música Brasileira](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/premio-da-musica-brasileira.html) (since 1987; organiser: Independent production (José Maurício Machline)): Formerly Prêmio Sharp and Prêmio TIM; the most traditional, with a critics' jury and categories by genre. Each edition honours a great name.
- [MTV Video Music Brasil (VMB)](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/mtv-video-music-brasil-vmb.html) (since 1995; organiser: MTV Brasil (1995–2012)): For almost two decades, the award that defined Brazilian pop and rock for the young.
- [Troféu Imprensa](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/trofeu-imprensa.html) (since 1958; organiser: SBT (Silvio Santos)): A TV award with best male and female singer categories, voted by journalists and the public.
- [WME Awards](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/wme-awards.html) (since 2017; organiser: Women's Music Event): An award dedicated to women in Brazilian music, across every role in the industry.
- [Prêmio Profissionais da Música](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/premio-profissionais-da-musica.html) (since 2015; organiser: Independent): Recognizes producers, engineers, backing musicians and other backstage professionals.
- [Prêmio Jovem Brasileiro](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/premio-jovem-brasileiro.html) (since 2002; organiser: Independent): Aimed at a young audience; music, TV and internet categories.
- [Troféu Promessas](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/trofeu-promessas.html) (since 2011; organiser: Geo Eventos and TV Globo): A gospel music award held with TV Globo's support from 2011 to 2013.
- [Grammy](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/awards/grammy.html) (since 1959; organiser: Recording Academy (US)): The American award where “Getz/Gilberto” was Album of the Year in 1965; Sérgio Mendes, Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil have also won.

## Festivals

- [Rock in Rio](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/rock-in-rio.html) (since 1985; city: Rio de Janeiro): Created by Roberto Medina; the 1985 edition launched BRock and the festival became a global franchise (Lisbon, Madrid, Las Vegas).
- [Lollapalooza Brasil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/lollapalooza-brasil.html) (since 2012; city: São Paulo): The Brazilian edition of the American festival, at the Interlagos racetrack.
- [Festa do Peão de Barretos](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/festa-do-peao-de-barretos.html) (since 1955; city: Barretos (SP)): Latin America's biggest rodeo and sertanejo's main stage.
- [Carnaval do Rio](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/carnaval-do-rio.html) (since 1932; city: Rio de Janeiro): Samba school parades at the Sambadrome (since 1984) and hundreds of street blocos.
- [Carnaval de Salvador](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/carnaval-de-salvador.html) (since 1950; city: Salvador): Trios elétricos on the Barra-Ondina and Campo Grande circuits; the world's biggest street party according to Guinness.
- [Carnaval de Recife e Olinda](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/carnaval-de-recife-e-olinda.html) (since 1907; city: Recife / Olinda): Frevo, maracatu and the Galo da Madrugada, the planet's biggest street bloco.
- [São João de Campina Grande e Caruaru](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/sao-joao-de-campina-grande-e-caruaru.html) (since 1983; city: Campina Grande (PB) / Caruaru (PE)): Thirty days of forró; the two cities compete for the title of 'biggest São João in the world'.
- [Festival de Parintins](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/festival-de-parintins.html) (since 1965; city: Parintins (AM)): The Garantido and Caprichoso bulls face off at the Bumbódromo, in the middle of the Amazon.
- [Abril Pro Rock](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/abril-pro-rock.html) (since 1993; city: Recife): The festival that revealed manguebeat.
- [Universo Paralello](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/universo-paralello.html) (since 2000; city: Pratigi (BA)): A beach psytrance festival at New Year, with an international crowd.
- [Festival de Verão Salvador](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/festival-de-verao-salvador.html) (since 1999; city: Salvador): Showcase of axé and Bahian pop.
- [Coala Festival](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/coala-festival.html) (since 2014; city: São Paulo): Dedicated solely to Brazilian music, with unprecedented cross-generational meetings.
- [Rec-Beat](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/rec-beat.html) (since 1995; city: Recife): An independent-music stage inside Recife carnival.
- [Festival Bananada](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/festival-bananada.html) (since 1999; city: Goiânia): The festival that made Goiânia a capital of indie and stoner.
- [Planeta Atlântida](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/planeta-atlantida.html) (since 1996; city: Xangri-lá (RS)): Summer festival on the Rio Grande do Sul coast.
- [João Rock](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/joao-rock.html) (since 2002; city: Ribeirão Preto (SP)): One of the biggest Brazilian rock festivals outside the capitals.
- [Villa Mix](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/villa-mix.html) (since 2011; city: Goiânia): A sertanejo universitário mega-festival.
- [The Town](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/the-town.html) (since 2023; city: São Paulo): Rock in Rio's sister festival, at Interlagos.
- [Festival Internacional da Canção (FIC)](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/festival-internacional-da-cancao-fic.html) (since 1966; city: Rio de Janeiro): Held by Globo until 1972; it launched 'Sabiá', 'Pra Não Dizer Que Não Falei das Flores' and 'BR-3'.
- [Festival da TV Excelsior](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/festival-da-tv-excelsior.html) (since 1965; city: São Paulo): The 1965 festival where Elis Regina sang “Arrastão” and became the great revelation of Brazilian song.
- [Free Jazz Festival](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/free-jazz-festival.html) (since 1985; city: Rio de Janeiro / São Paulo): Sixteen editions between 1985 and 2001, with jazz and Brazilian music side by side.
- [Hollywood Rock](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/hollywood-rock.html) (since 1988; city: Rio de Janeiro / São Paulo): Conceived by Nelson Motta; after a one-off edition in 1975, it ran from 1988 to 1996.
- [Skol Beats](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/skol-beats.html) (since 2000; city: São Paulo): The country's biggest electronic music festival of its time, from 2000 to 2008.
- [TIM Festival](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/tim-festival.html) (since 2003; city: Rio de Janeiro / São Paulo): The successor to Free Jazz, with jazz, indie, electronic music and rock.
- [Planeta Terra Festival](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/planeta-terra-festival.html) (since 2007; city: São Paulo): An indie and alternative festival held from 2007 to 2013.
- [Festival de Inverno de Campos do Jordão](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/festival-de-inverno-de-campos-do-jordao.html) (since 1970; city: Campos do Jordão (SP)): The country's great annual classical music festival, every July.
- [Festival de MPB da Record](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/festivals/festival-de-mpb-da-record.html) (since 1966; city: São Paulo): Until 1969; 'A Banda', 'Disparada', 'Alegria, Alegria' and 'Ponteio' came out of here.

## TV shows

- [The Voice Brasil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/the-voice-brasil.html) (network: Globo, SBT; years: 2012–2023, 2025–): Twelve seasons on Globo, from 2012 to 2023; coaches over the years included Carlinhos Brown, Claudia Leitte, Lulu Santos, Daniel, Michel Teló, Ivete Sangalo, Iza and Gaby Amarantos, and Michel Teló won as a coach seven times. In 2025 the show moved to SBT, where Thiago Garcia, from Mumuzinho's team, won. Artists who came through it: Ellen Oléria, Sam Alves, Danilo Reis & Rafael, Renato Vianna, Mylena Jardim, Samantha Ayara, Léo Pain, Tony Gordon, Victor Alves, Giuliano Eriston, Keilla Júnia, Ivan Barreto, Thiago Garcia, Ju Moraes, Liah Soares, Lucy Alves, Romero Ribeiro, Ayrton Montarroyos, Nikki Valentine, Carol Biazin, Day, Vinícius D'Black, Hugo Rafael.
- [The Voice Kids](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/the-voice-kids.html) (network: Globo; years: 2016–2023): The children's version, with coaches such as Carlinhos Brown, Ivete Sangalo, Simone & Simaria, Michel Teló, Gaby Amarantos and Mumuzinho.
- [The Voice +](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/the-voice.html) (network: Globo; years: 2021–2022): The version for singers over 60.
- [Popstars](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/popstars.html) (network: SBT; years: 2002–2003): Formed Rouge (2002), Brazil's biggest girl group, and the boy band Br'oz (2003). Artists who came through it: Rouge, Br'oz.
- [Fama](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/fama.html) (network: Globo; years: 2002–2005): A music reality show in the Spanish 'Operación Triunfo' format.
- [Ídolos](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/idolos.html) (network: SBT (2006–07) e Record (2008–12); years: 2006–2012): The Brazilian 'Pop Idol'; judges included Rick Bonadio, Arnaldo Saccomani, Marco Camargo and Paula Lima. Thaeme (2007) went on to sertanejo with Thaeme & Thiago. Artists who came through it: Thaeme.
- [Astros](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/astros.html) (network: SBT; years: 2008–2013): A newcomers' talent show hosted by Marcos Mion and Rodrigo Faro.
- [SuperStar](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/superstar.html) (network: Globo; years: 2014–2016): A band competition with app voting; winners were Malta (2014), Dois Africanos (2015) and Versalle (2016). Scalene was runner-up in 2015. Artists who came through it: Malta, Scalene, Versalle.
- [X Factor Brasil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/x-factor-brasil.html) (network: Band; years: 2016): A single season; the girl group Ravena won. Artists who came through it: Ravena.
- [Canta Comigo](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/canta-comigo.html) (network: Record; years: 2018–): The 'All Together Now' format with 100 judges, hosted by Rodrigo Faro; it has a Teen version.
- [The Masked Singer Brasil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/the-masked-singer-brasil.html) (network: Globo; years: 2021–): Celebrities sing in masks; hosted by Ivete Sangalo and later Eliana.
- [Estrelas da Casa](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/estrelas-da-casa.html) (network: Globo; years: 2024): A music confinement reality show created by Globo, formerly called Estrela da Casa.
- [Covernation](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/covernation.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 2005–2007): A duel between cover bands hosted by Marcos Mion, with two seasons in the regular schedule.
- [Show de Calouros](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/show-de-calouros.html) (network: Tupi, Record, REI e SBT; years: 1977–1996, 2024–): Silvio Santos's amateur talent show, with a panel of artists; it returned in 2024 as a segment of Programa Silvio Santos, hosted by Patrícia Abravanel.
- [Jovem Guarda](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/jovem-guarda.html) (network: Record; years: 1965–1968): Roberto Carlos, Erasmo Carlos and Wanderléa's show, which gave the movement its name. Artists who came through it: Roberto Carlos, Erasmo Carlos, Wanderléa.
- [Globo de Ouro](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/globo-de-ouro.html) (network: Globo; years: 1972–1990): TV's hit parade, featuring the artists behind the most-played songs.
- [Som Brasil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/som-brasil.html) (network: Globo; years: 1981): Rolando Boldrin's show devoted to caipira and sertanejo music.
- [Ensaio](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/ensaio.html) (network: TV Tupi e TV Cultura; years: 1969): Fernando Faro's interview and music show with the great names of MPB.
- [O Fino da Bossa](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/o-fino-da-bossa.html) (network: Record; years: 1965–1967): Hosted by Elis Regina and Jair Rodrigues; its success led to three live LPs.
- [Programa Raul Gil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/programa-raul-gil.html) (network: Record, Tupi, Manchete, Band e SBT; years: 1973): Raul Gil's live-audience show; it launched in 1973 on Record and later aired on Tupi, Manchete, Band and SBT. Artists who came through it: Robinson Monteiro.
- [Roberto Carlos Especial](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/roberto-carlos-especial.html) (network: Globo; years: 1974–): Roberto Carlos's year-end special, on air since 1974; it only skipped 1999.
- [Viola, Minha Viola](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/viola-minha-viola.html) (network: TV Cultura e TV Brasil; years: 1980–2019): The caipira music show, hosted by Inezita Barroso from 1980 to 2014.
- [Grandes Nomes](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/grandes-nomes.html) (network: Globo; years: 1980–1981): A monthly music series devoted to one great name of Brazilian music per episode.
- [Cassino do Chacrinha](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/cassino-do-chacrinha.html) (network: Globo; years: 1982–1988): Chacrinha's Saturday-afternoon live-audience show on TV Globo.
- [Galpão Crioulo](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/galpao-crioulo.html) (network: RBS TV; years: 1982–): An RBS TV programme on air since 1982, hosted by the nativist singers Nico Fagundes and later Neto Fagundes.
- [Fábrica do Som](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/fabrica-do-som.html) (network: TV Cultura; years: 1983–1984): A music programme made with Sesc, hosted by Tadeu Jungle.
- [Clip Clip](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/clip-clip.html) (network: Globo; years: 1984–1987): A Sunday music show hosted by the puppets Muquirana Jones and Edgar Ganta.
- [Mixto Quente](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/mixto-quente.html) (network: Globo; years: 1986): A Sunday-afternoon music festival in the summer of 1986, inspired by Rock in Rio.
- [Clip Trip](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/clip-trip.html) (network: TV Gazeta; years: 1989–1994): A daily music-video show hosted by Beto Rivera.
- [Som Pop](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/som-pop.html) (network: TV Cultura; years: 1989–1993): A music-video show hosted by Kid Vinil.
- [Disk MTV](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/disk-mtv.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 1990): Launched on 22 October 1990, right after MTV Brasil went on air; the Brazilian version of Dial MTV and one of the channel's biggest hits.
- [Top 20 Brasil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/top-20-brasil.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 1990–2006, 2013): MTV Brasil's music-video chart, on air from the channel's launch.
- [Yo! MTV](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/yo-mtv.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 1990–2006): The first Brazilian TV programme devoted to rap.
- [Lado B](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/lado-b.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 1991–2000): MTV's midnight show, hosted by Luiz Thunderbird, Soninha Francine, Fabio Massari and Kid Vinil.
- [Acústico MTV](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/acustico-mtv.html) (network: MTV Brasil): The Brazilian version of MTV Unplugged: bands and artists playing their songs acoustically.
- [Programa Livre](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/programa-livre.html) (network: SBT; years: 1991–2001): An SBT talk show hosted by Serginho Groisman from 1991 to 1999.
- [TVZ](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/tvz.html) (network: Multishow; years: 1993–): Multishow's prime-time music-video show, on air since 1993.
- [Acervo MPB](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/acervo-mpb.html) (network: TVE Brasil e TV Brasil; years: 1996–): MPB concerts shown in full, recorded exclusively by the broadcaster.
- [Luau MTV](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/luau-mtv.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 1996–2012): MTV acoustic concerts, on and off from 1996 to 2012; the first host was Cuca Lazzarotto.
- [Piores Clipes do Mundo](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/piores-clipes-do-mundo.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 1999–2002): Comedy built on questionable music videos, with Marina Person, Marcos Mion and João Gordo.
- [Demo MTV](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/demo-mtv.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 2000–2001): A showcase for Brazilian independent bands and their videos.
- [Musikaos](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/musikaos.html) (network: TV Cultura; years: 2000–2003): A music programme hosted by Gastão Moreira, with 143 episodes.
- [Gordo a Go-Go](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/gordo-a-go-go.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 2000–2005): João Gordo's talk show, one of MTV's big ratings winners.
- [Altas Horas](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/altas-horas.html) (network: Globo; years: 2000–): Serginho Groisman's Saturday-night talk show.
- [Um Barzinho, Um Violão](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/um-barzinho-um-violao.html) (network: Multishow; years: 2001): Big names of MPB and pop rock singing classics; it became a series of albums.
- [ClipMania](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/clipmania.html) (network: Band; years: 2001–2004): A music show hosted by Sabrina Parlatore.
- [Estúdio Coca-Cola](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/estudio-coca-cola.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 2007): Unlikely musical meetings: artists from different worlds on the same stage for the first time.
- [O Som do Vinil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/o-som-do-vinil.html) (network: Canal Brasil; years: 2007–): Hosted by musician and researcher Charles Gavin, on air since 2007.
- [Terra Nativa](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/terra-nativa.html) (network: Band; years: 2007): A music show hosted by the sertanejo duo Guilherme & Santiago.
- [Samba na Gamboa](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/samba-na-gamboa.html) (network: TV Brasil; years: 2008–2022, 2024–): The many forms of samba and MPB, with Diogo Nogueira until 2022 and Teresa Cristina since 2024.
- [Top 10 MTV](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/top-10-mtv.html) (network: MTV Brasil; years: 2008, 2010–2013): The ten music videos most voted by viewers online; a spin-off of Disk MTV.
- [Esquenta!](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/esquenta.html) (network: Globo; years: 2011–2017): Regina Casé's Sunday-afternoon live-audience show.
- [Mix Ao Vivo](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/mix-ao-vivo.html) (network: Mix TV): Concerts where bands played classic albums live, such as RPM with "Rádio Pirata".
- [Música Boa Ao Vivo](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/musica-boa-ao-vivo.html) (network: Multishow; years: 2014–): A music show hosted over the years by Thiaguinho, Anitta, Iza and Ivete Sangalo.
- [SóTocaTop](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/sotocatop.html) (network: Globo; years: 2018–2020): A Saturday-afternoon music show with hosts such as Luan Santana, Iza and Ludmilla.
- [Circuito Sertanejo](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/circuito-sertanejo.html) (network: Globo e Multishow; years: 2022–): A variety show focused on sertanejo and modão.
- [Bem Brasil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/bem-brasil.html) (network: TV Cultura): Live Brazilian music concerts, recorded first at USP and later at Sesc, hosted by Wandi Doratiotto.
- [Cultura Livre](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/cultura-livre.html) (network: TV Cultura): Artists from the contemporary alternative circuit, hosted by Roberta Martinelli.
- [Sr. Brasil](https://brazilianmusic.biblioverse.org/shows/sr-brasil.html) (network: TV Cultura, SescTV e TV Brasil): A Brazilian music programme created, directed and hosted by Rolando Boldrin.

## Instruments

- Pandeiro (Percussion; used in: Samba, Choro, Forró): A frame drum with jingles played by hand; the 'complete drum kit' of samba and choro.
- Tamborim (Percussion; used in: Samba): A small drum struck with a multi-rod stick; it plays the rhythmic figures of the samba schools.
- Surdo (Percussion; used in: Samba, Axé and Bahian Music): The deep bass drum that marks samba's second beat; the heart of the bateria.
- Cuíca (Percussion; used in: Samba): A friction drum with an inner rod that 'cries' and 'laughs'; samba's unmistakable sound.
- Agogô (Percussion; used in: Samba, Axé and Bahian Music): Two or more metal bells of different pitches, of Yoruba origin.
- Repinique / hand repique (Percussion; used in: Samba): A high-pitched drum that calls the bateria; in pagode it is played by hand.
- Tantã (Percussion; used in: Samba): A deep hand drum created in Fundo de Quintal's pagode to replace the surdo.
- Cavaquinho (Strings; used in: Samba, Choro): A small four-steel-string instrument, cousin of the ukulele; it plays the rhythmic harmony of samba and choro.
- Seven-string guitar (Strings; used in: Choro, Samba): A guitar with an extra low string for the bass runs of choro and samba.
- Viola caipira (Strings; used in: Sertanejo, Forró): Ten strings in five courses, a Portuguese inheritance; the voice of caipira music and repente.
- Bandolim (mandolin) (Strings; used in: Choro): Choro's soloist since Jacob do Bandolim; Hamilton de Holanda plays the ten-string version.
- Guitarra baiana (Strings; used in: Axé and Bahian Music): A long-neck electric cavaquinho invented by Dodô & Osmar for the trio elétrico.
- Berimbau (Strings; used in: Folk Traditions, Jazz and Instrumental): An African-origin musical bow with a gourd resonator; it leads the capoeira circle and entered jazz with Naná Vasconcelos.
- Sanfona / accordion (Keys; used in: Forró, Folk Traditions): Luiz Gonzaga's instrument; in the South, the button 'gaita-ponto' leads the vanerão.
- Zabumba (Percussion; used in: Forró): A shallow bass drum played with a mallet and a thin stick; the base of the forró trio.
- Triangle (Percussion; used in: Forró): The third member of the forró trio, marking the high-pitched time.
- Rabeca (Strings; used in: Forró): A rustic northeastern fiddle used in forró and rural maracatu.
- Pífano (Winds; used in: Forró): A bamboo flute of the pífano bands of the rural Northeast.
- Alfaia (Percussion; used in: Forró, Brazilian Rock): A rope-tuned wooden drum of maracatu, played with thick sticks; it electrified manguebeat.
- Timbau (Percussion; used in: Axé and Bahian Music): A light, high-pitched conical drum popularized by Carlinhos Brown and Timbalada.
- Atabaque (Percussion; used in: Axé and Bahian Music, Folk Traditions): The Afro-Brazilian drum of candomblé, capoeira and the afro blocos.
- Ganzá and chocalho (Percussion; used in: Samba, Forró): Metal or gourd shakers that fill out samba and coco.
- Reco-reco (Percussion; used in: Samba): A spring or bamboo scraper found in samba and afoxé.
- Curimbó (Percussion; used in: Brega, Calypso and Sounds of Pará): A hollowed-log drum that gives Pará's carimbó its name.
- Matraca and pandeirão (Percussion; used in: Folk Traditions): Wooden clappers and giant frame drums of Maranhão's bumba-meu-boi.
- Apito (whistle) (Winds; used in: Samba): The three-tone whistle of the bateria master commands the samba school.
- Berrante (cattle horn) (Winds; used in: Sertanejo, Folk Traditions): A horn made of ox horns, blown by drovers to lead the herd; it echoes in sertanejo songs and at rodeos.
- Viola de cocho (Strings; used in: Folk Traditions): A viola carved from a single piece of wood, accompanying siriri and cururu in Mato Grosso.
- Viola machete (Strings; used in: Samba): The small viola of the samba de roda of Bahia's Recôncavo.
- Plate and knife (Percussion; used in: Samba): A plate scraped with a knife, keeping the rhythm of samba de roda.
- Caixa (snare drum) (Percussion; used in: Samba): The snare drum of the samba school batería.
- Banjo (Strings; used in: Samba): A banjo with a cavaquinho neck and tuning, popularized in Fundo de Quintal's pagode.
- Caxixi (Percussion; used in: Folk Traditions, Axé and Bahian Music): A woven-straw shaker filled with seeds, accompanying the berimbau in capoeira.
- Afoxé (instrument) (Percussion; used in: Axé and Bahian Music): A gourd wrapped in a net of beads, shaken or twisted in the hands.
- Xequerê (Percussion; used in: Axé and Bahian Music): A large bead-covered gourd of Yoruba origin.
- Maracá (Percussion; used in: Indigenous Music): A gourd rattle used in the rituals of many Indigenous peoples.
- Tambor de crioula drums (Percussion; used in: Folk Traditions): The three drums (grande, meião and crivador) of the tambor de crioula dance in Maranhão.

### Popular instruments used in Brazilian music

- Acoustic guitar (Strings; used in: Samba, Bossa Nova, MPB, Sertanejo): The most played instrument in the country; the base of samba, bossa nova, MPB and sertanejo, from João Gilberto and Baden Powell to Yamandu Costa.
- Electric guitar (Strings; used in: Brazilian Rock, Brega, Calypso and Sounds of Pará): Arrived with Jovem Guarda and Tropicália and became the voice of rock and of Pará's guitarrada.
- Electric bass (Strings; used in: MPB, Brazilian Rock, Soul and Black Music): From Luizão Maia's swing with Elis Regina to Champignon's slap in Charlie Brown Jr.
- Double bass (Strings; used in: Bossa Nova, Jazz and Instrumental): The foundation of samba-jazz and of bossa nova trios.
- Violin (Strings; used in: Classical Music, Sertanejo): Found in orchestras, in romantic sertanejo arrangements and in northeastern armorial music.
- Drum kit (Percussion; used in: Samba, Brazilian Rock, Jazz and Instrumental): Luciano Perrone and Edison Machado adapted samba to the kit; from samba-jazz to Sepultura's metal.
- Piano and keyboard (Keys; used in: Bossa Nova, MPB, Forró): From Tom Jobim's and Johnny Alf's piano to the keyboard of electronic forró and piseiro.
- Synthesizer (Keys; used in: Brazilian Rock, Brazilian Funk, Brega, Calypso and Sounds of Pará, Electronic): Defined 1980s pop-rock and underpins funk, tecnobrega and electronic music.
- Saxophone (Winds; used in: Choro, Samba, Soul and Black Music): Pixinguinha moved to tenor sax in the 1940s; heard in choro, gafieira and Banda Black Rio's soul.
- Flute (Winds; used in: Choro, Jazz and Instrumental): Choro's soloist since the 19th century, from Pixinguinha to Altamiro Carrilho.
- Clarinet (Winds; used in: Choro, Forró): A voice of choro and of frevo orchestras; Abel Ferreira and Paulo Moura.
- Trumpet (Winds; used in: Forró, Axé and Bahian Music, Samba): The brass of frevo, gafieira, axé and electronic forró.
- Trombone (Winds; used in: Jazz and Instrumental, Forró, Samba): Raul de Souza took the Brazilian trombone into jazz; essential in frevo and gafieira.
- Harmonica (Winds; used in: Brazilian Rock, Samba): The harmonica of blues and rock; Rildo Hora brought it into samba.

## Glossary

- **Abadá**: The T-shirt that grants access to a trio elétrico bloco.
- **Afoxé**: A candomblé-linked carnival procession, such as Filhos de Gandhy.
- **Agronejo**: Sertanejo with funk and agribusiness pride, from the 2020s.
- **Ao vivo**: A hallmark of today's market: in 2025, 27 of the country's 50 most-played songs were live recordings.
- **Aparelhagem**: The giant sound system of Belém's parties; the stage of tecnobrega.
- **Arrocha**: A romantic Bahian ballad danced close together.
- **Axé**: A Yoruba word for life force; the name of the Bahian genre of the 1980s.
- **Baile**: The funk party, usually in a community court or street; 'baile funk' became an international term.
- **Baião**: The northeastern rhythm launched nationally by Luiz Gonzaga in 1946.
- **Balada**: A night out or club; also a romantic 'balada', the slow song.
- **Batalha de rima**: An improvised rap contest in public squares, such as Batalha da Aldeia.
- **Bateria**: In a samba school this is not the drum kit: it is the percussion section with hundreds of players.
- **Batidão**: Any heavy, danceable beat in funk or pop.
- **Bloco**: A group that parades in street carnival; Salvador's afro blocos created samba-reggae.
- **Bossa**: Rio slang for 'knack' or 'charm'; 'bossa nova' is the new way of playing samba from 1958.
- **Brega**: From 'cafona' (tacky); popular romantic music of the 1960s–80s that became a genre with pride.
- **Breque**: A stop in the samba where the singer speaks a line; it names samba de breque.
- **BRock**: 1980s Brazilian rock, named by journalist Arthur Dapieve.
- **Caipira**: A country dweller of rural São Paulo and Minas; caipira music is the root of sertanejo.
- **Cantoria**: A gathering of repente singers in the Northeast.
- **Catira**: A caipira dance of handclaps and foot-stamping to the viola.
- **Chamamé**: An accordion rhythm from the Argentina and Paraguay border.
- **Choro**: An urban instrumental genre from late 19th-century Rio; also called chorinho.
- **Clube da Esquina**: The Minas collective of Milton Nascimento and Lô Borges and their 1972 album.
- **CTG**: Centre of Gaúcho Traditions, where Rio Grande do Sul's music is played and danced.
- **Disco de ouro**: Pro-Música Brasil certification for sales or streams.
- **Dupla**: Two singers acting as one name, usually in thirds: sertanejo's classic line-up.
- **ECAD**: The office that collects and distributes public-performance royalties in Brazil.
- **Enredo**: The theme of a samba school's parade, told by its samba-enredo.
- **Escola de samba**: A carnival association that parades with a samba-enredo, floats and a bateria; Mangueira, Portela, Salgueiro.
- **Fandango**: A viola and rabeca dance of caiçara communities and the South.
- **Feminejo**: The wave of women in sertanejo from 2015 on.
- **Festa junina**: June festivals (St Anthony, St John, St Peter) with forró and square dancing; Campina Grande and Caruaru hold the biggest.
- **Festival**: The TV Record and Globo song festivals (1965–72) launched MPB.
- **Forró**: From 'forrobodó', a lively party; it does not come from 'for all', as the legend says.
- **Frevo**: The frantic rhythm of Recife carnival; 'to boil' in Pernambuco speech.
- **Funk**: In Brazil this is not American funk: it is funk carioca, an electronic beat born at Rio dance parties.
- **Gafieira**: A popular dance hall; it names samba de gafieira, with horns.
- **Gravadora**: Record label; the majors and the independents (Deckdisc, Midas, Som Livre).
- **Gênero de fusão**: A genre born from mixing two or more styles, such as funknejo (funk + sertanejo) or tecnobrega (brega + electronic music); in Portuguese, gênero de fusão. Crossover is something else: an artist or song reaching the audience of another genre.
- **Ijexá**: A candomblé rhythm played in afoxé processions.
- **Intérprete**: A singer who does not write; Elis Regina and Gal Costa were great interpreters.
- **Iê-iê-iê**: What Brazilians called 1960s rock, after the Beatles' 'yeah, yeah, yeah'.
- **Jongo**: A circle dance with Bantu-rooted drums from the Southeast.
- **Jovem Guarda**: A TV Record show (1965–68) and the youth-rock movement of Roberto and Erasmo Carlos.
- **Letrista**: The lyric writer; Vinicius de Moraes and Aldir Blanc are the most celebrated.
- **Louvor**: Evangelical worship music; Brazilian 'worship'.
- **Mandelão**: São Paulo funk of the 2020s with distorted bass and 'automotivo'.
- **Manguebeat**: Recife movement of the 1990s: maracatu + rock + hip-hop, with Chico Science.
- **Maracatu**: An Afro-Brazilian procession, 'de nação' (urban) or rural ('de baque solto'), in Pernambuco.
- **MC**: Master of ceremonies: the one who sings in funk and rap.
- **Mestre-sala e porta-bandeira**: The couple who carry the samba school's flag in the parade.
- **Micareta**: Off-season carnival with trio elétrico.
- **Modão**: Classic, sorrowful 'roots' sertanejo; the opposite of universitário.
- **MPB**: Música Popular Brasileira: not a rhythm but the songwriting tradition born at the 1960s festivals.
- **Ostentação**: São Paulo funk of 2011–14 about cars, brands and money.
- **Pagode**: Two things: the backyard samba circle (and the style born from it in the 1980s) and, in Bahia, the danceable pagode baiano.
- **Pagodão**: Another name for pagode baiano, with a fast beat.
- **Paredão**: A powerful car sound system at street parties, linked to funk and arrocha.
- **Partido-alto**: Samba with a fixed chorus and improvised verses in a circle.
- **Passinho**: A Rio street dance born at funk parties.
- **Pipoca**: Those who follow the trio elétrico outside the ropes, without an abadá.
- **Piseiro**: Sped-up electronic forró of the 2020s, with the 'pisadinha' keyboard.
- **Proibidão**: Funk with explicit or crime-related lyrics, outside the radio circuit.
- **Pé-de-serra**: Traditional trio forró: accordion, zabumba and triangle.
- **Regional**: The ensemble that plays choro: flute or mandolin, cavaquinho, guitars and pandeiro.
- **Repente**: Rhymed improvisation by two duelling viola players.
- **Roda de samba**: An informal gathering around a table where everyone sings and plays.
- **Samba de roda**: The samba of Bahia's Recôncavo, sung and danced in a circle.
- **Sambódromo**: The samba school parade avenue; Rio's opened in 1984.
- **Sanfoneiro**: An accordion player; the central figure of forró.
- **Sarau**: A poetry and music gathering, today strong in the outskirts and in rap.
- **Saudade**: The untranslatable word for the loving absence of someone or something; the theme of half of Brazilian songs.
- **Sertão**: The semi-arid interior of the Northeast; 'sertanejo' means 'from the sertão', though the genre comes from the Centre-South.
- **Slam**: A spoken-poetry competition born from hip-hop: poets recite their own texts and the audience scores them. In English, poetry slam; the broader, non-competitive form is spoken word.
- **Sofrência**: Heartbreak sertanejo (and arrocha) about drink and betrayal; Marília Mendonça was the 'queen of sofrência'.
- **Tamborzão**: The sampled atabaque beat that defined 2000s funk carioca.
- **Toada**: The boi-bumbá song, sung at the Parintins Festival.
- **Trio elétrico**: A truck with stage and sound system that leads the bloco at Salvador carnival.
- **Tropicália**: The 1967–68 movement that joined Brazilian music, electric guitars and avant-garde.
- **Universitário**: Sertanejo born at student parties in Goiás and Paraná in the 2000s; poppier and faster.
- **Xote**: Forró's slow, partner-danced rhythm, from the German 'Schottisch'.
